title: The conflict with no markers: one side deleted the file
summary: You edited a module; someone else deleted it. Git cannot express that as markers inside a file, so it hands you a decision instead — and the wrong choice is silent.
mental_model: Content conflicts get markers because both sides have text. A modify/delete conflict has no text on one side, so git leaves the file in the tree, marks it conflicted, and waits for you to say 'keep it' or 'delete it'.

commit.message: Extend legacy migration for v2 customers
Add a helper on main too

steps.title: See the collision coming
steps.why: One branch deleted legacy.py and added helper.py; the other extended legacy.py and added a different helper.py. Two different kinds of conflict in one merge.

steps.title: Merge and read the two conflict types
steps.why: The messages differ: one says 'deleted in feature/cleanup and modified in HEAD', the other is a normal add/add content conflict. Only the second has markers in the file.
steps.expect: DU or UD for legacy.py, AA for helper.py.

verify.label: the merge is stopped on the deleted file

steps.title: Look inside — there is nothing to look at
steps.why: legacy.py is sitting in your working tree exactly as main had it, with no markers. That is the trap: it looks resolved. If you just `git add` it without thinking, you have silently overruled the deletion.
steps.expect: The full file, no markers, no obvious sign of a conflict.

steps.title: Inspect the three stages to see what is missing
steps.why: `ls-files -u` shows the unmerged stages: 1 base, 2 ours, 3 theirs. legacy.py has stages 1 and 2 but no stage 3 — proof, in one line, that their side deleted it.
steps.expect: Two rows for legacy.py, three for helper.py.

steps.title: Decide: the deletion was wrong
steps.why: main extended the file for v2 customers who still exist, so keeping it is the correct call. `git add` on a modify/delete conflict is how you say 'keep the file'.

verify.label: the modify/delete conflict is resolved
verify.hint: git add legacy.py to keep it

steps.title: Resolve the add/add conflict properly
steps.why: helper.py exists on both sides with different content, so it does get markers. Combine the two intentions rather than picking one — the usual right answer for an add/add.

steps.title: Restore the import the other side removed
steps.why: Their commit removed the import along with the file. Keeping the file means the import belongs back — merge resolution is a code review, not a file-picking exercise.

verify.label: the modify/delete conflict was resolved by keeping the file
verify.hint: git add legacy.py keeps it; git rm legacy.py would accept the deletion

verify.label: …including the v2 extension that made it worth keeping
the add/add conflict has no leftover markers
both sides' helpers survived
verify.hint: an add/add conflict usually wants combining, not choosing

verify.label: the import was restored to match the decision to keep the file

pitfalls: A modify/delete conflict leaves an ordinary-looking file on disk. `git add` means keep, `git rm` means accept the deletion — there is no third option and no marker to remind you.
`git status --short` codes: DU deleted by us, UD deleted by them, AA both added, UU both modified. The letters are the fastest read of what happened.
Accepting a deletion often leaves imports and callers behind. The compiler catches it in a typed language; in Python it is a runtime error in production.
`git checkout --ours <file>` does nothing useful on a modify/delete conflict, because one side has no version of the file at all.
cheatsheet: DU/UD/AA/UU tell you the conflict type
the unmerged stages: 1 base, 2 ours, 3 theirs
